## What happened during the period?

The income statement explains revenue earned and expenses incurred during a period. Net income is not the same as cash received: accrual accounting records performance when earned or incurred.

Read vertically for margins and horizontally for multi-year trends. Ask: Did revenue grow? Did gross margin change? Which operating costs grew faster than sales? Are unusual gains or losses included?

### A useful distinction

Depreciation lowers profit now but usually does not use cash in the same period. The cash-flow statement reconciles this difference later.

The balance sheet is measured at a particular date. Compare several year-ends and connect changes to the cash-flow statement and notes.

## The one equation worth memorising

**Assets = liabilities + equity.** Every transaction preserves this relationship. Assets are resources controlled by the company; liabilities are obligations; equity is the residual claim of owners.

Use this first: before trusting a figure, identify the reporting entity, reporting period, currency, unit (for example, millions), and reporting framework.

> Teaching heuristic (not a rule): if a number looks surprising, first check the unit, period, and whether it is a stock (point in time) or a flow (over a period).

### Try it

A founder invests $100 cash. Assets increase by $100 and equity increases by $100. No revenue has been earned.

## Where did cash actually go?

Operating cash flow starts from business operations. Investing cash flow covers long-lived investments and acquisitions. Financing cash flow covers lenders and owners.

Free cash flow is a useful *analytical measure*, not a universally defined accounting line item. Always write the formula you use and inspect capital-expenditure assumptions.

### Reconciliation habit

When net income and operating cash flow diverge, inspect non-cash charges and working-capital movements. A one-year gap may be normal; a persistent unexplained gap deserves investigation.

## Read the opinion precisely

An unmodified opinion is not a guarantee that a business is healthy or fraud-free. It is an opinion on whether the financial statements are presented fairly, in all material respects, under the relevant framework.

Pay attention to the opinion type, going-concern disclosures, and key audit matters. Then find the associated notes and form your own questions.

## Build a chain of evidence

Compare at least three periods. Link revenue, margins, working capital, operating cash flow, capital expenditure, debt, dilution, and note disclosures. A ratio is a prompt for a question—not a verdict.

### Capstone workflow

2. Trace the main changes through all three statements.
3. Read the supporting notes, audit report, and management narrative.
